newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Fernz deals Rhone-Poulenc strategic blow.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Fernz deals Rhone-Poulenc strategic blow.

text.p: New Zealand's Fernz Corporation has dealt French chemicals goliath Rhone-Poulenc a strategic blow in a battle for control of a burgeoning agri- chemicals market, managing director Kerry Hoggard said.

Hoggard told Reuters on Monday he expects Rhone-Poulenc will probably sell its 32 percent stake in industrial chemicals group Compagnie Francaise des Produits Industriels (CFPI) after Fernz' bought the founding Hess family's shares last week.
Buying the strategic 17 percent stake took Fernz' total equity holding in CFPI to 45.14 percent, and Hoggard said he did not believe Rhone-Poulenc would now retain its minority holding.
"I don't think either company is in a situation where they're going to sit there with a minority position on a long term basis," he said in a telephone interview.
Fernz intends to launch a takeover bid for the remaining shares at 380 French francs per share. The offer values all of CFPI at NZ$139 million (US$96 million).

Rhone-Poulenc indicated as recently as last November it was interested in taking control of CFPI. While it is still possible for Rhone to make a counter-bid, Hoggard was confident Fernz will secure control of CFPI at its offer price.

Fernz has been wrestling Rhone, the seventh largest pharmaceutical and chemical group in the world, for control of CFPI because it is the key to the international market for agricultural chemical bromoxynil.
Bromoxynil is used as a herbicide to protect small and coarse grains.
Rhone supplies about 80 percent of the bromoxynil market worldwide, and a takeover of CFPI, which holds the remaining 20 percent, would have given it total control of the product.

That could have had implications for Fernz, because it supplies 80 percent of the world market for MCPA, another agricultural chemical which is used almost exclusively in conjuction with bromoxynil, Hoggard explained.
If Fernz succeeded in taking control of CFPI it would be in a stronger position to work with Rhone to distribute sales of both products.
Hoggard said Fernz had identified CFPI as a takeover target 12 months ago because of its involvement in the agricultural and industrial chemicals businesses internationally.
He said that within CFPI's NZ$370 million annual turnover, 45 percent was from agricultural chemical sales and 55 percent from industrial chemical sales.
Fernz' business is now solely focused on those two areas following the company's exit last week from its direct investment in fertiliser production.
"We've been building an international agricultural chemicals operation for the last five years," Hoggard said.
"What we're endeavouring to do as part of that strategy is to take positions in certain key strategic chemicals which are important in the international marketplace."
Hoggard said Fernz was looking at further acquisitions, including an international agricultural chemicals company and two Australasian industrial chemical operations, one of which was in New Zealand.
Fernz posted a NZ$43.5 million (US$30 million) profit in the year to May 31, 1996. Rhone-Poulenc's 1996 net income was 2.74 billion French francs (US$484 million).
